To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

researchers strongly endorse obligations to provide study participants with subsequent access to updated research information and relevant clinical care, but also report barriers to care, especially for participants with ASD, and that researchers' attitudes about cascading obligations are influenced by the nature of the results reported and by their own professional characteristics.
researchers endorse cascading obligations to provide updated information and clinical care, and that they perceive significant barriers to providing clinical care to participants in ASD research.

researchers involved in ASD and CF genetic research endorse the idea that research teams should have a responsibility to help ensure that participants have access to relevant information and clinical care after receiving research results, but they also believe that there are barriers to fulfilling this responsibility.

the researchers we surveyed strongly endorsed the obligation to report research results to study subjects, and they strongly endorsed the obligation for researchers to ensure access to updated information or relevant care for participants.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

researchers perceive a strong obligation to report research results to participants, and that they also perceive a strong obligation for research teams to ensure participants have access to updated information and relevant clinical care, but that there are barriers to this access.

researchers endorse cascading obligations to ensure participants have access to updated information and relevant clinical care following any report of research results, but that researchers are less confident that these cascading obligations can be fulfilled in practice.
the research community is not yet prepared to address the cascade of obligations associated with the reporting of genetic research results to participants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the obligation to report research results to study volunteers is not the end of the story.
researchers are not just debating whether they should communicate research results to participants; they are also grappling with the cascade of obligations that might flow from any initial report.

the debate about whether and when to report genetic research results should not be divorced from the broader question of whether and how researchers are obligated to ensure access to updated information and relevant clinical care.
